title: RIC-specific cytoprotective profile mediated by microglia in a mouse model of acute ischaemic stroke.
abstract: Background: Remote ischaemic conditioning (RIC) is an endogenous neuroprotective strategy involving repeated, transient occlusion of a limb artery to reduce ischaemic injury at a distant site. We investigated the effects of RIC in a mouse model of focal cerebral ischaemia induced by distal transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO). Animals were randomised into three groups: Stroke (tMCAO, 60 min), Stroke+remote ischaemic preconditioning (RIPerC) (RIC applied during ischaemia) and Stroke+remote ischaemic postconditioning (RIPostC) (RIC initiated 10 min after reperfusion). The RIC protocol consisted of three cycles of 5-minute hindlimb ischaemia followed by 5-minute reperfusion. Results: At 72 hours postischaemia, both RIPerC and RIPostC significantly reduced the infarct volumes in male and female mice. In males, infarct size decreased from 6.31 ± 0.28% (Stroke) to 3.77 ± 0.47% (RIPerC, p<0.0025) and 4.00 ± 0.40% (RIPostC, p<0.0061). However, the RIPerC+RIPostC group significantly increased the infarct volume compared with the Stroke group (8.41± 0.72%). In females, reductions were greater: from 6.69±0.46% (Stroke) to 2.95 ± 0.34% (RIPerC, p<0.0001) and 2.96 ± 0.32% (RIPostC, p<0.0001). Functional recovery was improved, particularly with RIPostC, correlating with infarct size reduction (Pearson’s r=0.5505 in males, r=0.7313 in females). Apoptosis was reduced by over 50% with both treatments, and microglial phagocytic activity (cluster of differentiation 68+/Iba1+ (ionised calcium binding adaptor molecule 1)) increased significantly. Microglial depletion using PLX3397 (71.3% reduction in Iba1+ cells) worsened ischaemic injury, yet RIC preserved its protective effects, suggesting additional microglia-independent mechanisms. Furthermore, RIC enhanced neurogenesis in the subventricular zone and infarct core (doublecortin marker+ cells doubled versus Stroke), with a marked proliferative response in female hippocampi (Ki67+ cells increased by 127%). Conclusion: These findings reveal sex-specific efficacy of RIC, with mechanistic insights obtained in male animals suggesting a dual mode of action via modulation of microglial function and promotion of endogenous neurorepair pathways.

title: Sequential blood-brain barrier-penetrating and microglial-mitochondria-targeting nanosystem for ischemic stroke therapy.
abstract: Ischemic stroke (IS) causes severe neurological deficits closely linked to microglial overactivation after ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury, a process governed by mitochondrial homeostasis. However, restoring microglial mitochondrial function across the blood-brain barrier (BBB) remains challenging. Here, we report a sequentially targeted nanosystem, M-BPM@TGPB, for I/R injury therapy. It comprises a triphenylphosphonium (TPP)-modified, gadolinium-doped Prussian blue core and a mannose-modified BV2-platelet hybrid membrane shell. This design integrates mannose for BBB penetration, platelet membrane for lesion targeting, BV2 membrane for microglial uptake, and TPP for mitochondrial localization, enabling precise vascular-to-subcellular delivery. In vitro, the nanosystem crossed the BBB, localized to BV2 mitochondria, scavenged reactive oxygen species (ROS), restored mitochondrial function, and inhibited inflammation. In a mouse model of middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO/R), the intravenously administered nanosystem accumulated in microglial mitochondria, scavenged mitochondrial ROS (mtROS), restored mitochondrial homeostasis, promoted M1-to-M2 polarization, suppressed neuroinflammation, reduced neuronal apoptosis, and promoted angiogenesis, thereby reducing infarct volume from 36.61% to 10.57% and the modified neurological severity score (mNSS) from 14 to 2.5. It also exhibited favorable biocompatibility and enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) contrast. Critically, rather than broadly scavenging ROS, this strategy specifically restores microglial mitochondrial function, shifting the therapeutic focus from general antioxidant approaches to organelle-specific intervention. This work may offer a promising design paradigm for nanotherapies targeting central nervous system disorders in which mitochondrial dysfunction and neuroinflammation are core pathological drivers.

title: Beyond Blood-Brain Barrier Crossing in Reperfusion-Era Ischemic Stroke: Interface-Matched Active-Entity Delivery and Translational Product Design.
abstract: Reperfusion therapy has transformed acute ischemic stroke care, yet large-vessel recanalization does not ensure capillary reperfusion, preservation of the blood-brain barrier and neurovascular unit (BBB/NVU), or durable neurological recovery. Nanomedicine is still commonly judged by BBB crossing or ischemic-hemisphere accumulation, although vascular access, tissue viability, transport phenotype, thromboinflammation, and standard treatment change rapidly during the lifetime of a formulation. This narrative review proposes a conceptual framework that matches the reperfusion state and pathological interface to the compartment in which the therapeutically active entity must act. The framework is intended to organize preclinical evidence and generate testable translational hypotheses; it has not yet been clinically validated. Persistent occlusion may favor intravascular targets, whereas recanalization with no-reflow creates a distinct microvascular delivery problem. Early reperfusion injury may prioritize BBB/NVU stabilization, while later biological contexts may require selective immune, regenerative, or organelle-directed interventions. These contexts may coexist spatially, vary across vascular territories, and shift during treatment; they should therefore not be interpreted as a mandatory chronological sequence. We distinguish BBB crossing, controlled barrier modulation, and BBB/NVU repair as separate therapeutic tasks, and introduce transport attrition as a practical explanation for why sequential targeting, transcytosis, cellular uptake, endosomal escape, and organelle localization can yield little final active-entity exposure despite strong tissue imaging. Recent predominantly preclinical examples illustrate how thrombus-targeted rtPA systems, neutrophil-intercepting particles, NET-degrading polymersomes, lesion-targeted nanoplatforms, and mitochondrial nanomedicines may fit different delivery topologies. Translational credibility requires topology-resolved exposure, target engagement in viable tissue, hemocompatibility under antithrombotic treatment, state-appropriate models, function-linked manufacturing controls, and compatibility with thrombolysis and thrombectomy.

title: Neutrophil extracellular traps in ischemic stroke: Thrombolysis resistance, no-reflow, and hemorrhagic transformation.
abstract: Recanalization is central to acute ischemic stroke treatment. However, reopening an occluded artery does not always restore microvascular perfusion, and hemorrhagic transformation (HT) can occur regardless of recanalization success. Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) may help explain these discordant outcomes because they act within occlusive thrombi, the downstream microcirculation, and the neurovascular interface. This review examines the roles of NETs in thrombolysis resistance, no-reflow, and hemorrhagic injury. Within thrombi, NET-associated chromatin reinforces clot architecture and limits fibrinolysis. Intravascular NETs may impede downstream microvascular flow after recanalization, while NET-related inflammatory signaling may aggravate blood-brain barrier disruption and HT. These findings implicate NETs in impaired recanalization, incomplete tissue reperfusion, and hemorrhagic injury and support their evaluation as an adjunctive target during reperfusion therapy.

title: Mitochondrial cristae remodeling in ischemic stroke: mechanisms and therapeutic perspectives.
abstract: Mitochondrial cristae arrange the respiratory machinery within the inner membrane and change as ischemia gives way to reperfusion. Their organization depends on mitochondrial contact site and cristae organizing system assemblies, optic atrophy 1, adenosine triphosphate synthase, and cardiolipin. Disruption of these systems can impair energy production, facilitate neuronal death, and expose mitochondrial DNA to inflammatory sensors. This review brings structural work together with experimental stroke studies to examine how crista remodeling contributes to injury and recovery. Genetic manipulation of selected regulators has preserved mitochondrial structure and reduced injury in neurons and microglia. Most of these interventions preceded ischemia, leaving the speed and feasibility of repair after stroke onset uncertain. Pharmacological modulation and mitochondrial delivery offer ways to address this gap, particularly around reperfusion. Emerging strategies combine modulation of crista protein assemblies with cardiolipin directed treatment, mitochondrial antioxidant nanomedicine, organelle delivery, and control of local drug exposure. Their therapeutic evaluation can be aligned with distinct opportunities at reperfusion and during subsequent tissue recovery. Progress toward treatment will require evidence that a candidate reaches the affected brain cells, modifies the intended membrane assembly, and produces lasting neurological benefit. The available studies place crista remodeling within neuroprotective pathways and identify the experimental steps needed to evaluate it as a therapeutic target.

title: Characterization and treatment of ischemic stroke in patients with infective endocarditis: a meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Ischemic stroke is a common and serious complication of infective bacterial endocarditis. This study aimed to characterize the frequency, clinical and pathological features, treatment strategies, and outcomes of patients with stroke due to infective endocarditis.

METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed from database inception to October 2022 for studies reporting on stroke in patients with infective endocarditis and performed a meta-analysis.

RESULTS: A total of 122 studies comprising 270,211 patients with infective endocarditis were included. Ischemic stroke occurred in 21% and hemorrhagic stroke in 5% of patients. Stroke was observed in 32% of patients with mitral valve endocarditis, 25% with aortic valve, and 11% with tricuspid valve endocarditis. Stroke was associated with significantly higher mortality (OR 2.35; 95%CI 1.74-3.16). Staphylococcus and Streptococcus species were most frequently associated with stroke (33% and 25%, respectively). The risk of stroke did not differ significantly between patients with and without pre-existing antithrombotic therapy (37% vs. 24%; OR 1.24, 95%CI 0.75-2.06). Successful reperfusion was achieved in 80% of patients undergoing mechanical thrombectomy, although mortality remained high at 49%.

CONCLUSIONS: Stroke is a common complication of infective bacterial endocarditis and has a substantial impact on patient outcomes. It occurs most frequently in patients with mitral valve endocarditis and in those with infections caused by staphylococcal pathogens. Stroke risk was not reduced in patients with pre-existing antithrombotic therapy, supporting discontinuation where no other indication exists. Mechanical thrombectomy in patients with endocarditis-related large vessel occlusion achieves high recanalization rates; however, overall clinical outcomes remain poor in this population.

This study aimed to characterize the frequency, clinical and pathological features, treatment strategies, and outcomes of patients with stroke due to infective endocarditis. METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed from database inception to October 2022 for studies reporting on stroke in patients with infective endocarditis and performed a meta-analysis.

title: Mitochondrial calpain-1 cleaves MAVS and controls inflammation in cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury.
abstract: Calpains are calcium-activated cysteine proteases present in the cytoplasm and mitochondria that are essential to physiological processes; however, the functions of calpain-1 in the brain are not well understood. Therefore, we explored novel calpain-1 substrates using the GPS-CCD software package. Calpain inhibitors, calpeptin and Tat-μCL, suppressed cleavage of mitochondrial antiviral signaling protein (MAVS) in the presence of exogenous calcium. Moreover, calpain-1 knockout mice suppressed MAVS cleavage in cerebral ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury. These findings indicate that MAVS is a novel calpain-1 substrate. As MAVS degradation prevents inflammation, its cleavage might contribute to the suppression of inflammation in I/R injury.

title: Calycosin alleviates blood-brain barrier disruption after cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury by inhibiting NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis.
abstract: Ischemic stroke, a severe neurological disorder with a multifactorial pathogenesis, presents significant therapeutic challenges. Calycosin, a natural flavonoid, has diverse biological activities, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antitumor effects. In this study we investigate the protective effects of calycosin against blood-brain barrier (BBB) damage following cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) and explore the underlying mechanisms. We employ middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) in rats and oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) in bEnd.3 brain microvascular endothelial cells to assess neurological function, BBB integrity, the expression of pyroptosis-related proteins, inflammatory mediator release, endothelial barrier permeability, and cell viability. The results reveal that calycosin significantly ameliorates CIRI-induced BBB damage, as evidenced by improved neurological scores, reduced brain water content, and decreased infarct volume. Calycosin suppresses NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis by downregulating HMGB1, NLRP3, caspase 1, GSDMD, N-GSDMD, and IL-18 expression while reducing the secretion of HMGB1, IL-1β, and IL-18. Additionally, calycosin enhances BBB integrity by decreasing MMP9 and AQP-4 expression and upregulating the expression of tight junction proteins (ZO-1, occludin, and claudin-5). In OGD-treated bEnd.3 cells, calycosin inhibits NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis, reduces inflammatory mediator release, and improves cell viability and barrier function. Notably, molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate that calycosin stably binds to NLRP3 with high affinity, supporting its potential as an NLRP3 inhibitor. These findings indicate that calycosin protects against CIRI-induced BBB damage by inhibiting NLRP3-mediated pyroptosis and modulating tight junction protein expression, indicating that calycosin is a potential therapeutic option for ischemic stroke.

Calycosin, a natural flavonoid, has diverse biological activities, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antitumor effects. In this study we investigate the protective effects of calycosin against blood-brain barrier (BBB) damage following cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) and explore the underlying mechanisms.

title: [Acute management of minor ischemic stroke].
abstract: This review summarizes acute-phase treatment for minor ischemic stroke, focusing on the latest evidence for reperfusion therapy and acute antithrombotic treatment. In patients with large vessel occlusion, the benefit of mechanical thrombectomy is not established and the risk of hemorrhage exists; therefore, indications should be judged carefully for each patient. Intravenous thrombolysis provides limited benefit in non-disabling cases, and dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) can be an option. For minor non-cardioembolic stroke, early DAPT is recommended, and the possible role of adding argatroban is promising, especially for suspected branch atheromatous disease. For cardioembolic stroke, early initiation of a direct oral anticoagulant is desirable in mild cases without a large infarct.

title: Neuroprotective effect by splenic hypothermia in ischemic stroke.
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To investigate whether spleen-targeted remote administration of hypothermia (RAH) modulates splenic neutrophil release, attenuates neutrophil-driven cerebral inflammation, and preserves BBB integrity at early reperfusion after stroke.

METHODS: Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent 2-h middle cerebral artery occlusion followed by 6-, 24- and 48- h of reperfusion. RAH was applied to the splenic region via surface cooling, with 1-min cycles administered at 5-min intervals. Neurological deficits, infarct volume, neutrophil infiltration, cytokine expression, BBB integrity, and apoptosis were assessed using neurobehavioral scoring, TTC staining, Western blotting, rt-PCR, immunofluorescence, ELISA, and TUNEL, respectively.

RESULTS: RAH rapidly reduced splenic temperature from 370 to 28 °C without altering body or brain temperatures. At 6 h reperfusion, splenic neutrophil release was suppressed and brain neutrophil infiltration decreased. RAH reduced early elevations of TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6. At 24 h, anti-inflammatory effects persisted and BBB integrity was preserved, restoring tight-junction and matrix proteins and suppressing BBB-damaging mediators. Compared to non-RAH stroked rats, RAH reduced apoptosis, body weight loss (9.1 ± 2.8 vs. 19.7 ± 7.2 g, p < 0.05), infarct volume (33.9 ± 4.1% vs. 53.6 ± 1.9%, p < 0.05), cerebral edema (11.2 ± 0.9% vs. 16.3 ± 1.3%, p < 0.05) and Evans blue extravasation (4.8 ± 0.2 vs. 9.8 ± 0.2 mg/g, p < 0.05), and improved neurological outcomes. RAH attenuated stroke-induced spleen weight loss and contraction, consistent with reduced splenic neutrophil mobilization.

CONCLUSIONS: RAH induces neuroprotection after ischemic stroke by suppressing splenic neutrophil activation and mobilization, thus attenuating peripheral-to-central inflammatory trafficking and preserving BBB integrity. These findings highlight spleen-targeted cooling may represent a promising early intervention to ischemic stroke.

METHODS: Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent 2-h middle cerebral artery occlusion followed by 6-, 24- and 48- h of reperfusion. RAH was applied to the splenic region via surface cooling, with 1-min cycles administered at 5-min intervals.

title: Essential oil from Angelica sinensis Radix attenuates ischemic stroke via the cGMP/PKG/MAPK pathway: insights from network pharmacology and molecular mechanism evaluation.
abstract:
ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: As a traditional herbal remedy, the root of Angelica sinensis has long been used to treat headaches, strokes, and dementia. As the primary active ingredient in A. sinensis, A. sinensis essential oil (ASEO) also plays a significant role in the therapy of stroke. Although ASEO has shown clear therapeutic effects, its specific mechanism of preventing ischemic stroke still needs to be further clarified.

AIM OF THE STUDY: Through network pharmacological analysis combined with in vitro and in vivo experimental verification, this study investigated the protective effects of ASEO against stroke and elucidated the underlying molecular regulatory mechanisms.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) was used to analyze the chemical composition of ASEO. Middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO/R) rats were administered different doses of ASEO to evaluate its therapeutic effects. The therapeutic effects were evaluated using behavioral, histopathological, and immunofluorescence assays. In addition, using network pharmacology techniques, the potential molecular mechanisms underlying the treatment of ischemic stroke with ASEO have been preliminarily elucidated. HT22 cells treated with oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R) were used as an in vitro model. Subsequently, the key signal transduction pathways involved in the therapeutic effects of ASEO against ischemic stroke were further validated using multiple experimental approaches, including enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), flow cytometry, Western blotting, pathway-specific pharmacological inhibition and PKG-specific siRNA knockdown.

RESULTS: Twenty-seven compounds were identified from ASEO by GC-MS. In vivo experiments demonstrated that ASEO treatment exerted significant protective effects on MCAO/R rats by improving impaired neurological function, reducing cerebral infarct volume, alleviating neuronal apoptosis, and modulating the expression of apoptotic proteins. Mechanistically, network pharmacology studies suggested that the protective mechanism of ASEO may involve the cGMP/PKG and MAPK signaling pathways. Subsequent experiments confirmed that ASEO inhibited neuronal apoptosis via the cGMP/PKG/MAPK axis both in vivo and in vitro. Importantly, both pharmacological inhibition and siRNA-mediated genetic knockdown of PKG significantly attenuated the protective effects of ASEO against OGD/R injury in HT22 cells.

CONCLUSION: ASEO exerts its anti-ischemic stroke effect by attenuating apoptosis via the cGMP/PKG/MAPK signaling pathway, providing a scientific foundation for its clinical application in ischemic stroke therapy.

title: Pharmacological basis of Suhexiang Wan in ischemic stroke: identification and functional characterization of piperlongumine as a brain-distributed bioactive constituent associated with STAT3-mediated blood-brain barrier protection.
abstract:
ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Suhexiang Wan (SHXW) is a classical traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) formula that has been traditionally used for stroke-related disorders, including sudden loss of consciousness, neurological dysfunction, and hemiplegia. Although modern pharmacological studies have suggested its neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory properties, the brain-distributed constituents potentially associated with its therapeutic effects in ischemic stroke (IS) and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear.

AIM OF THE STUDY: This study aimed to elucidate the pharmacological basis of SHXW in IS by identifying brain-distributed constituents and investigating a candidate constituent potentially associated with its protective effects against cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury (CIRI), with particular emphasis on blood-brain barrier (BBB) protection.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: SHXW-derived constituents detected in brain tissue under middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO/R) conditions were characterized using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS). Integrated network pharmacology analysis was performed to predict potential therapeutic targets and signaling pathways. Piperlongumine (PIP) was further confirmed and quantified in SHXW and brain tissue using an authentic standard-based LC-MS/MS approach. Molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, biophysical binding assays, and cellular target-engagement experiments were used to investigate the interaction between PIP and signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3). The protective effects and associated mechanisms were evaluated in a mouse MCAO/R model and an oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R)-induced brain microvascular endothelial cell injury model.

RESULTS: Among 1991 putatively annotated constituents of SHXW, 55 SHXW-derived constituents were detected in brain tissue under MCAO/R conditions. In the MCAO/R mouse model, SHXW significantly improved neurological deficits, reduced infarct volume and brain edema, decreased BBB permeability, and restored tight junction protein expression. Among the brain-detected constituents, PIP, a natural alkaloid derived from Piper longum L., was selected for further investigation based on its detection in brain tissue, network topology characteristics, predicted association with STAT3, and reported pharmacological relevance to ischemic injury. Authentic standard-based LC-MS/MS confirmed PIP in SHXW and brain tissue, with a PIP content of 48.21 ± 1.10 μg/g in SHXW and a brain concentration of 159.67 ± 8.37 ng/g at 2 h after SHXW administration. Biophysical and cellular target-engagement assays supported the interaction between PIP and STAT3. PIP partially recapitulated the protective effects of SHXW by alleviating neurological deficits, preserving BBB integrity, restoring endothelial barrier function, and suppressing STAT3-associated inflammatory responses. STAT3 knockdown partially phenocopied the endothelial protective effects of PIP, whereas restoration of STAT3 expression in STAT3-knockdown cells reversed the protective phenotype. PIP treatment attenuated the injury-associated changes following STAT3 restoration, supporting the functional involvement of STAT3-associated signaling in PIP-mediated BBB protection.

CONCLUSIONS: This study provides new insights into the pharmacological basis of SHXW in IS by integrating chemical profiling, brain distribution analysis, and pharmacological validation. SHXW exerted protective effects against CIRI and preserved BBB integrity. Among the SHXW-derived constituents detected in brain tissue, PIP was identified and functionally characterized as a bioactive candidate associated with BBB protection. The findings support the involvement of PIP-STAT3 interaction and STAT3-associated inflammatory signaling in PIP-mediated BBB protection. These results provide pharmacological evidence linking the traditional application of SHXW with its modern molecular mechanisms while highlighting brain-distribution-guided approaches for investigating the therapeutic basis of complex TCM formulas.

title: Puerarin preserves microglial homeostasis and protects against acute cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury by regulating autophagy and oxidative stress through Janus kinase 2/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Microglial oxidative stress and dysregulated autophagy contribute to secondary neuronal injury following ischemic stroke. Puerarin (PUE), a bioactive isoflavone with established antioxidative and neuroprotective properties, may protect against cerebral ischemia by modulating microglial dysfunction; however, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.

METHODS: The neuroprotective effects of PUE were investigated in a rat transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) model and in BV2 microglia subjected to oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R). Microglial phenotypic alterations, oxidative stress, and autophagic activity were evaluated using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), ultrastructural, biochemical, and fluorescence-based analyzes. Data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomics, pharmacological gain- and loss-of-function approaches, and adeno-associated virus serotype 9 (AAV9)-mediated Janus kinase 2 (JAK2) knockdown were employed to define the role of Janus kinase 2/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (JAK2/STAT3) signaling. Microglia-mediated neuroprotection was further assessed using an HT22 neuron-microglia co-culture system.

RESULTS: PUE reshaped the microglial landscape by preserving the homeostatic microglial phenotype while suppressing ischemia-induced pathological activation. PUE reduced intracellular and mitochondrial ROS production, restored redox homeostasis, suppressed excessive autophagosome formation, and downregulated the autophagy-related proteins 3/5/12 (ATG3/5/12). Mechanistically, these protective effects were mediated through inhibition of JAK2/STAT3 signaling. Genetic silencing of JAK2 recapitulated the effects of PUE, whereas pharmacological activation of JAK2/STAT3 largely abolished its antioxidative, anti-autophagic, and neuroprotective activities. Furthermore, conditioned media from PUE-treated microglia significantly alleviated neuronal injury in HT22 cells, supporting a microglia-mediated paracrine mechanism of neuroprotection.

CONCLUSION: Collectively, these findings identify JAK2/STAT3-dependent regulation of the oxidative stress-autophagy axis as a critical mechanism underlying microglial homeostasis after acute cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) and establish PUE as a promising therapeutic candidate for ischemic stroke.

Puerarin (PUE), a bioactive isoflavone with established antioxidative and neuroprotective properties, may protect against cerebral ischemia by modulating microglial dysfunction; however, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. METHODS: The neuroprotective effects of PUE were investigated in a rat transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) model and in BV2 microglia subjected to oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R).

title: Outcomes of Intra-Arterial Urokinase After Endovascular Reperfusion for Acute Ischemic Stroke Due to Cardioembolism: A Secondary Analysis of the POST-UK Trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Whether adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis improves outcomes in patients with acute ischemic stroke due to cardioembolism remains unclear. This study aimed to investigate the efficacy and safety of adjunctive intra-arterial urokinase in patients with acute ischemic stroke due to cardioembolism who achieved near-complete to complete reperfusion.

METHODS: This study was a secondary analysis of the POST-UK (Adjunctive Intra-Arterial Urokinase After Near-Complete to Complete Reperfusion for Acute Ischemic Stroke) trial, which was conducted from November 15, 2022, to March 29, 2024. Patients were randomly assigned to the intra-arterial urokinase group or the control group. The primary outcome was disability-free survival at 90 days, defined as a modified Rankin Scale score of 0 to 1. Safety outcomes included 90-day all-cause death, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage and any intracranial hemorrhage within 48 hours.

RESULTS: Among 209 patients with cardioembolism (median age 73 [interquartile range, 63-81] years; 45.9% men), 106 were assigned to the control group and 103 to the intra-arterial urokinase group. Compared with the control group, adjunctive intra-arterial urokinase significantly increased the odds of disability-free survival at 90 days (adjusted risk ratio, 1.49 [95% CI, 1.08-2.06]; P=0.01; inverse probability of treatment weighting adjusted risk ratio, 1.47 [95% CI, 1.04-2.09]; P=0.03). No significant differences were found between groups in 90-day mortality rate, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage, or any intracranial hemorrhage within 48 hours.

CONCLUSIONS: In patients with acute ischemic stroke due to cardioembolism who achieved near-complete to complete reperfusion, adjunctive intra-arterial urokinase significantly improved disability-free survival at 90 days without increasing the risk of death or intracranial hemorrhage.

title: Continuous Near-Infrared Spectroscopy as a Real-Time Monitor of Intravenous Thrombolysis in Acute Ischaemic Stroke: A Prospective Observational Emergency Department Study.
abstract: Background. Intravenous (IV) thrombolysis is the standard of care for acute ischaemic stroke (AIS), yet there is still no objective bedside tool for monitoring the brain continuously during the infusion. Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) provides non-invasive, continuous measurement of regional cerebral oxygen saturation (rSO2). We evaluated whether bilateral frontal NIRS, and in particular the absolute interhemispheric difference in rSO2 (ΔNIRS), tracks the clinical trajectory of patients receiving IV alteplase in the emergency department (ED). Methods. A prospective observational cohort study was conducted in the ED of a tertiary university hospital. Consecutive adults receiving IV alteplase for AIS were screened, and those enrolled underwent continuous bilateral frontal NIRS monitoring. Bilateral rSO2, ΔNIRS, vital signs, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) were recorded at baseline and at 0, 15, 30, 45, 60 and 120 min after the start of the infusion. Patients were classified by clinical trajectory during monitoring as improvement, no change, or deterioration. Results. Forty-one patients were analyzed (26 female, 63.4%; mean age 73.6 ± 14.8 years); 15 (36.6%) improved, 21 (51.2%) showed no change and 5 (12.2%) deteriorated. In the whole cohort, absolute rSO2 rose only slightly in the affected hemisphere and did not change in the unaffected hemisphere. However, affected-hemisphere rSO2 rose significantly in the improvement group (median 59 to 67; p = 0.001) and fell significantly in the deterioration group (p = 0.015). ΔNIRS narrowed from a median of 4 (IQR 3-9) at baseline to 1 (IQR 0-5) at 120 min in the improvement group (p = 0.034) and did not change significantly in the other groups. The two patients with acute complications desaturated bilaterally. NIHSS correlated strongly and inversely with GCS at every time point (ρ = -0.74 to -0.84; all p < 0.001). Conclusions. During IV thrombolysis in the ED, continuous bilateral frontal NIRS tracked the clinical trajectory. Because recanalisation and reperfusion were not assessed independently, what NIRS paralleled was the clinical course, not reperfusion itself. These hypothesis-generating findings warrant larger studies that validate ΔNIRS against perfusion or vascular imaging.

title: Gut microbiota as a potential mediator of the disease-ameliorating effects of molecular hydrogen: mechanisms and therapeutic perspectives.
abstract: Molecular hydrogen (H2) has emerged as a promising bioactive gas with well-documented antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cytoprotective properties, and its therapeutic potential for a range of human diseases has been increasingly recognized. Accumulating evidence suggests that the gut microbiota (GM) may contribute to some of the biological effects of H2. The GM serves as both a key site for endogenous H2 production and consumption, and a potential site of interaction with exogenous H2 supplementation, with possible implications for intestinal microecological homeostasis. This narrative review critically summarizes current evidence on the bidirectional relationship between H2 and the GM, focusing on microbial H2 production and consumption, the potential role of H2 in maintaining gut microbial homeostasis, and the impact of exogenous H2 supplementation on intestinal microecology. The potential therapeutic relevance of H2-associated GM modulation is further discussed in metabolic diseases, gastrointestinal disorders, and neurodegenerative diseases. Proposed mechanisms include regulation of microbial composition, reinforcement of intestinal barrier integrity, suppression of inflammation and oxidative stress, modulation of microbial metabolites, and gut-organ axis signaling. Collectively, current evidence supports that H2 may influence the GM ecosystem. However, most supporting data remains preclinical, and whether GM alterations causally mediate the biological or therapeutic effects of H2 remains to be established. Elucidating the reciprocal interaction between H2 and the GM may provide new mechanistic insight into H2-based interventions and facilitate the development of microbiota-targeted therapeutic strategies for human diseases.

title: Central retinal artery occlusion preceding hemispheric ischemic stroke treated with mechanical thrombectomy: A case report.
abstract:
RATIONALE: Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is a form of ischemic stroke that may signal underlying cerebrovascular or cardiac disease.

PATIENT CONCERNS: A 52-year-old man developed sudden, painless vision loss in the right eye. Nine days later, he presented with left-sided weakness and speech difficulty, with a National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score of 8. His medical history included dilated cardiomyopathy, and electrocardiography revealed atrial fibrillation.

DIAGNOSES: Ophthalmologic examination and fluorescein angiography supported right CRAO. Computed tomography (CT) angiography at neurological presentation showed right internal carotid artery occlusion from its origin. CT perfusion demonstrated estimated infarct core and penumbral volumes of 37 and 186 mL, respectively.

INTERVENTIONS: Emergency mechanical thrombectomy with aspiration and adjunctive balloon angioplasty achieved expanded Thrombolysis in Cerebral Infarction grade 2c reperfusion.

OUTCOMES: The NIHSS score improved to 2 at discharge, 7 days after admission. At 3 months, the modified Rankin Scale score was 1, although right-eye visual loss persisted.

LESSONS: CRAO warrants prompt cerebrovascular and cardiac evaluation, with reassessment when new neurological deficits develop. The nine-day interval between retinal symptoms and thrombectomy does not establish the duration of carotid occlusion or cerebral ischemia. The favorable individual outcome does not establish the efficacy of thrombectomy beyond 24 hours.

title: Zinc activates autophagy by regulating HDAC6 expression following cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury.
abstract: Intracellular zinc accumulation and excessive autophagy have been reported to contribute to neuronal death following cerebral ischemia/reperfusion (I/R). Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), which contains a zinc-dependent active site, is closely associated with autophagy. However, the relationship between zinc, HDAC6 and autophagy following cerebral I/R remains unclear. In this study, we aim to investigate whether ischemia-induced zinc accumulation activates autophagy through HDAC6. Rats were treated with zinc chelator, autophagy activator/inhibitor or HDAC6 inhibitor during a 90-minute middle cerebral artery occlusion. Infarct volume, neurological deficits, protein expression, and the colocalization of HDAC6, Beclin1, and zinc in neurons were evaluated. Our results demonstrate that beclin1 expression was significantly increased after cerebral I/R and this elevation was markedly attenuated by zinc chelation. Notably, reactivation of autophagy with rapamycin significantly, though not completely, diminished TPEN-mediated neuroprotection, suggesting that zinc-induced autophagy is an important contributor to neuronal injury following cerebral I/R. Moreover, immunofluorescence revealed that HDAC6 was colocalized with Beclin1 in the penumbra of ischemic rats, and inhibition of HDAC6 reduced Beclin1 expression and alleviated brain injury. Molecular docking analysis suggested a potential interaction between HDAC6 and α-tubulin, which may influence autophagy by regulating microtubule stability and autophagosome transport. Furthermore, chelating zinc decreased HDAC6 expression, while HDAC6 inhibition did not influence zinc levels, demonstrating that zinc acts upstream of HDAC6. In conclusion, our findings identify a novel zinc-HDAC6-autophagy signaling axis underlying neuronal injury following cerebral I/R, suggesting that targeting zinc homeostasis or HDAC6 may represent a promising therapeutic strategy.

Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), which contains a zinc-dependent active site, is closely associated with autophagy. title: Heterogeneity and risk assessment in minor ischemic stroke.
abstract: Minor ischemic stroke is often defined by a low National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score, yet patients with similar scores may have very different vascular lesions, tissue injury, and stroke mechanisms. This narrative review examines four domains that modify prognosis and management: symptom relevance, vascular and hemodynamic status, tissue status, and etiologic subtype. Adverse trajectories differ in timing. Early neurological deterioration (END) or infarct growth usually occurs within hours to days, recurrent ischemia clusters over days to weeks, and incomplete recovery may persist for months. A low NIHSS score may occur despite a disabling posterior-circulation or eloquent deficit, large- or medium-vessel occlusion, poor collateral flow, hypoperfusion, branch atheromatous disease, or an active embolic source. These outcomes are distinct from the mechanisms that drive them; high-risk minor stroke is not limited to large-vessel occlusion. PRISMS did not demonstrate benefit of alteplase over aspirin in selected patients with minor nondisabling stroke, ARAMIS found dual antiplatelet therapy noninferior to alteplase in a similarly selected population, and TEMPO-2 did not support routine tenecteplase in minor stroke selected by intracranial occlusion or focal perfusion abnormality. At ESOC 2026, MILD-MT investigators reported a higher proportion of patients achieving 90-day mRS 0-1 with endovascular therapy (EVT) plus best medical management than with best medical management alone in a selected group with anterior-circulation LVO, NIHSS <6, and favorable perfusion imaging. These findings are not directly comparable with TEMPO-2 because the intervention, imaging selection, reperfusion mechanism, time window, and outcome context differed. Short-course dual antiplatelet therapy remains supported for eligible non-cardioembolic minor stroke, while longer-term prevention should be tailored to the identified etiologic subtype. The modified Rankin Scale may miss residual deficits after minor stroke; measures such as the Canadian Outcome Scale for Minor Stroke (COSMOS) may capture performance, participation, and personally meaningful activities more sensitively. The four-domain framework is intended to organize clinical assessment, not to serve as a validated prediction score or treatment algorithm.

title: Brain cytoprotection in acute ischemic stroke in the reperfusion era: neuroimmune networks, clinical evidence, and translational barriers.
abstract: Intravenous thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy have transformed acute ischemic stroke (AIS) care, yet angiographic recanalization does not guarantee adequate tissue reperfusion or long-term functional independence. Brain cytoprotection has therefore expanded from neuron-centered rescue to preservation of the ischemic penumbra, neurovascular unit, blood-brain barrier (BBB), and microcirculation. Using a systems-immunology perspective, this clinically oriented narrative review examines ischemia-reperfusion injury as a dynamic network linking danger-associated molecular pattern sensing, microglia and astrocytes, circulating leukocytes, platelets and complement, endothelium and pericytes, cytokine signaling, edema, no-reflow, and regulated cell-death programs. We integrate classic and recent evidence for excitotoxic, redox and mitochondrial, inflammatory, barrier, microvascular, and cell-death targets; evaluate representative pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic interventions; and distinguish negative primary endpoints from exploratory subgroup or surrogate signals. Confirmatory excitotoxicity trials have remained negative overall. Selected multitarget agents have shown benefit in specific Chinese populations, whereas immune-, edema-, and no-reflow-directed approaches have yielded stage-specific but inconsistent safety, imaging, and functional results. Statins, nitric oxide donors, and phosphodiesterase inhibition have plausible vascular or immunomodulatory actions, but available trials do not establish them as acute cytoprotective therapies. Future development should align the right mechanism, tissue phenotype, treatment time, exposure, target-engagement measure, and patient-centered endpoint, followed by multicenter preclinical testing and independent cross-regional clinical replication. This end-to-end framework reframes brain cytoprotection as precision modulation of a spatially and temporally evolving neuroimmune-vascular system rather than a single undifferentiated treatment class.

title: Shenqi Granules Ameliorate Cerebral Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury by Regulating Glucocerebrosidase and Uridine Metabolism in Microglia.
abstract: Objective: Shenqi Granules is a traditional Chinese medicine formula derived from the classic prescription Shenqi Formula (SQF), composed of Astragali Radix (Huangqi) and Codonopsis Radix (Dangshen). SQF shows neuroprotection in cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI), but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Methods: The rat model of middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) was established using the suture method to evaluate the neuroprotective effect of SQF. Blood-absorbed components were identified via UHPLC-Q-TOF-MS/MS, and potential targets and pathways were predicted through network pharmacology. Non-targeted metabolomics of serum and feces was performed using UHPLC-Orbitrap MS, and core metabolic pathways were selected based on regulation magnitude (RM). Gut microbiota structure was analyzed by 16S rRNA sequencing, with associations between microbiota and metabolites assessed via the Mantel test and redundancy analysis (RDA). Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) was applied to screen core Hub genes for ischemic stroke (IS). Based on single-cell RNA data, a uridine transport/metabolism-associated transcriptional signature score (Uridine_Score) was constructed, and cell type-specific coupling between glucocerebrosidase (GBA) and this transcriptional signature was analyzed. Microglial temporal trajectory analysis was conducted using Monocle3. Molecular docking between core components and GBA was verified by AutoDock, and GBA mRNA expression was confirmed by RT-qPCR. Results: High-dose SQF reduced infarct volume and neuronal damage and improved behavior. A total of 28 absorbed components and 31 shared IS targets were identified. Metabolomics revealed nucleotide metabolism as a core pathway common to both serum and fecal samples. SQF restored gut-blood uridine balance (serum uridine 0.41× Sham → 0.85× post-SQF), reduced fecal dTMP and hypoxanthine. 16S rRNA sequencing demonstrated that the overall correlation between microbial community structure and nucleotide metabolites was statistically significant (Mantel r = 0.307-0.321, p < 0.01). WGCNA highlighted GBA, MMP9, and PYGL. Single-cell analysis showed a microglia-specific uridine transport/metabolism-associated transcriptional signature post-stroke, with GBA most correlated with this signature (ρ = 0.377). Pseudotime revealed microglial state transitions (Homeostatic → Acute_Reactive → DAM), with positive GBA-uridine transport/metabolism-associated transcriptional coupling in the Homeostatic and DAM states. Riboflavin showed the strongest GBA binding (-9.83 kcal/mol), and SQF upregulated GBA mRNA in the penumbra (p < 0.0001). Conclusions: SQF reprograms nucleotide metabolism via the gut-blood axis and enhances microglial GBA-uridine transport/metabolism-associated transcriptional coupling.

Methods: The rat model of middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) was established using the suture method to evaluate the neuroprotective effect of SQF.

title: Hydrogen sulfide inhibits neuroinflammation following cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury via regulating glial polarization.
abstract: Hydrogen sulfide (H2S), an endogenous gasotransmitter, exerts potent anti-neuroinflammatory effects. Both endogenous and exogenous H2S attenuate cerebral ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) injury by suppressing neuroinflammatory responses. Microglia play a pivotal role in post-ischemic neuroinflammation. Upon activation, microglia polarize toward either the pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype or the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype. The progression of neuroinflammation is closely associated with M1 polarization, while H2S has been demonstrated to inhibit M1 polarization and promote the protective M2 phenotype. Similarly, astrocytes undergo phenotypic transformation following ischemic stroke, with A1 reactive astrocytes exacerbating neuronal injury and A2 reactive astrocytes exerting neuroprotective effects. Our previous studies have shown that both endogenous and exogenous H2S promote astrocytic polarization toward the neuroprotective A2 phenotype. This review provides a comprehensive overview of ischemic stroke and the anti-neuroinflammatory effects of H2S and its donors in cerebral I/R injury, with particular emphasis on their roles in regulating microglial and astrocytic polarization toward neuroprotective phenotypes. Additionally, we discuss the intracellular signaling pathways involved in H2S-mediated suppression of neuroinflammation. Collectively, this review highlights the therapeutic potential of H2S donors as novel agents for the treatment of cerebral I/R injury. We propose that H2S donors exert their neuroprotective effects primarily through coordinated regulation of microglial and astrocytic polarization toward anti-inflammatory phenotypes, and that this dual-cell targeting strategy represents a viable therapeutic approach for cerebral I/R injury.

title: Risk factors and clinical outcomes of reocclusion after endovascular treatment for acute ischemic stroke: an updated systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Early reocclusion after endovascular treatment (EVT) for acute ischemic stroke is underrecognized; its determinants and impact remain poorly defined.

METHODS: Random-effects meta-analysis of early reocclusion after successful EVT (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library through January 2026). Crude odds ratios (ORs) were pooled and certainty rated with GRADE. Post hoc sensitivity analyses included only same-site reocclusion definitions.

RESULTS: Ten studies (3,381 patients) were included; 244 (7.2%) reoccluded. Reocclusion was associated with lower 90-day functional independence (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.17-0.38) and higher mortality (OR 1.86, 1.29-2.68), both moderate certainty. Reocclusion was more frequent with large-artery atherosclerosis (OR 2.24, 1.41-3.55; same-site 3.04, 1.73-5.33) and less frequent with cardioembolism (OR 0.40, 0.28-0.57) and atrial fibrillation (OR 0.39, 0.26-0.59), mutually confounded associations reflecting one embolic-versus-atherothrombotic axis. Prestroke antiplatelet therapy (OR 0.43, 0.28-0.67) lost significance under the same-site definition (0.60, 0.31-1.16). Exploratory data (two cohorts) linked eTICI 2c-3 reperfusion with less reocclusion (OR 0.44, 0.28-0.69). No study reported when etiology was adjudicated; the atherosclerosis association may be partly outcome-induced.

CONCLUSIONS: Early reocclusion is uncommon but carries a substantial prognostic penalty. Its determinants appear to lie in the vascular substrate rather than thrombectomy technique; prospective studies with uniform same-site definitions and systematic follow-up imaging are needed.

METHODS: Random-effects meta-analysis of early reocclusion after successful EVT (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library through January 2026). Crude odds ratios (ORs) were pooled and certainty rated with GRADE.

title: Reperfusion-sensitive induction of endothelial NDRG1 identifies a dynamic vascular stress response to thrombolysis in ischemic stroke.
abstract: Ischemic stroke (IS) outcome critically depends on the neurovascular unit's capacity to respond to ischemia-reperfusion stress within the salvageable penumbra. Here, we characterize the spatiotemporal regulation of N-myc downstream-regulated gene 1 (NDRG1) and identify it as an early, reperfusion-sensitive marker of endothelial stress. Under physiological conditions, NDRG1 is primarily expressed in neurons and oligodendrocytes, with minimal endothelial expression. Following middle cerebral artery occlusion, NDRG1 undergoes marked spatial and cellular redistribution, becoming strongly induced in endothelial cells across the cerebrovascular tree.Endothelial NDRG1 induction was detectable as early as 6 h after ischemia and evolved from a vesicular pattern to diffuse vascular labeling by 24 h. Importantly, recombinant tissue-type plasminogen activator (rtPA) selectively enhanced endothelial NDRG1 expression in peri-lesional vessels in the rtPA-sensitive thrombin model, but not in the rtPA-resistant FeCl3 model, indicating that NDRG1 induction is linked to effective reperfusion. In vitro, oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) recapitulated endothelial NDRG1 induction, further enhanced by rtPA through a pathway involving the LDL receptor family.Collectively, these findings identify endothelial NDRG1 as a dynamic molecular readout of reperfusion-sensitive vascular stress. NDRG1 may serve as a biomarker of endothelial responsiveness to thrombolytic therapy, providing new insight into cerebrovascular adaptations associated with successful reperfusion.

title: Role and mechanism of ATF6-mediated endoplasmic reticulum stress in ITLN-1 against cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury.
abstract:
AIMS: Intelectin-1 (ITLN-1), a novel adipocytokine, exerts neuroprotective effects against cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI), yet its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study focused on activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6), a key endoplasmic reticulum stress sensor, to explore its role in CIRI-induced neuronal injury and determine whether ITLN-1 mediates neuroprotection through ATF6 regulation.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: We established an N2a cell hypoxia/reoxygenation (H/R) model and a mouse middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) model. Using protein-protein molecular docking, in situ proximity ligation assay, Western blotting, mitochondrial membrane potential assays, and TUNEL staining, we investigated ATF6 activation in neuronal apoptosis and its upstream regulatory mechanisms.

KEY FINDINGS: H/R injury markedly induced ATF6 activation in N2a cells, triggering mitochondrial dysfunction and promoting apoptosis. ATF6 overexpression further aggravated these effects, supporting its critical pathogenic role in CIRI. Mechanistic analyses revealed that ITLN-1 physically associates with ATF6. Both ITLN-1 overexpression and exogenous recombinant ITLN-1 administration significantly suppressed excessive ATF6 activation, modulated the JNK signaling pathway, improved cell viability, reduced intracellular calcium overload and reactive oxygen species accumulation, and attenuated neuronal apoptosis. In vivo, ITLN-1 ameliorated neurological deficits, reduced neuronal damage, and alleviated demyelination, whereas ITLN-1 knockdown produced opposite effects.

SIGNIFICANCE: Excessive ATF6 activation underlies CIRI-induced neuronal injury. ITLN-1 exerts neuroprotection by inhibiting ATF6 and modulating JNK signaling, thereby alleviating mitochondrial dysfunction and reducing apoptosis. These findings highlight the ITLN-1/ATF6 axis as a promising therapeutic target for ischemic stroke.

title: Y-Configuration Dual Stent Retriever Thrombectomy for Bifurcation Occlusions in Acute Ischemic Stroke.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Bifurcation occlusions present unique technical challenges during mechanical thrombectomy. We evaluated the angiographic, clinical, and safety outcomes of Y-configuration dual stent retriever thrombectomy in patients with acute ischemic stroke caused by bifurcation occlusions.

METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 32 consecutive patients treated with Y-configuration dual stent retriever thrombectomy between April 2018 and January 2025. The technique was used as a rescue strategy after failed single-device attempts or as a first-line approach in selected bifurcation occlusions. Angiographic outcomes, procedural metrics, complications, and 90-day clinical outcomes were assessed.

RESULTS: The middle cerebral artery was the most common occlusion site (81.3%). Successful reperfusion (TICI ≥2b) was achieved in 97% of patients, with complete reperfusion (TICI 3) in 91% of cases. Following the first Y-configuration thrombectomy attempt, successful reperfusion (TICI ≥2b) was achieved in 87% of cases, irrespective of prior thrombectomy attempts. Median NIHSS improved from 16 at baseline to 7 at 24 hours. At 90 days, 53% of patients achieved functional independence (mRS ≤2). Symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 6.3%; any intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 9.4%, and no vasospasm, vessel dissection, device-related perforation, or subarachnoid hemorrhage was observed.

CONCLUSIONS: Y-configuration dual stent retriever thrombectomy appears feasible as a rescue option for selected complex bifurcation occlusions refractory to conventional thrombectomy. Prospective comparative studies are needed to further establish its safety, efficacy, and optimal indications.

We evaluated the angiographic, clinical, and safety outcomes of Y-configuration dual stent retriever thrombectomy in patients with acute ischemic stroke caused by bifurcation occlusions. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 32 consecutive patients treated with Y-configuration dual stent retriever thrombectomy between April 2018 and January 2025.

title: Neutrophil to Lymphocyte Ratio and Neurological Outcome in Ischemic Stroke at 4.5 to 24 Hours: A Post Hoc Analysis of TRACE-III Trial.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Whether neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio (NLR), as a marker of increased inflammatory response, modifies the efficacy and safety of tenecteplase is uncertain in patients 4.5-24 h after stroke onset. We investigated this in the Tenecteplase Reperfusion Therapy in Acute Ischemic Cerebrovascular Events-III (TRACE-III) trial.

METHODS: TRACE-III was a phase 3, multicenter, prospective, open-label, randomized, blinded-endpoint trial that enrolled 516 patients from 58 centers in China between January 2022 and November 2023. Patients had anterior large vessel occlusion and evidence of salvageable brain tissue on perfusion imaging, presented 4.5-24 h after symptom onset, and were randomized 1:1 to intravenous tenecteplase (intervention) or standard medical treatment (control). The primary efficacy and safety outcomes were modified Rankin scale score of 0-1 at 90 days and symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage or death, respectively. This post hoc analysis in 513 patients with complete admission NLR data compared outcomes in patients with elevated NLR (> first quartile) and non-elevated NLR (≤ first quartile).

RESULTS: In the elevated NLR group (> 3.0), tenecteplase was associated with increased functional independence (61 [30.2%] vs. 36 [19.6%]; adjusted relative rate [aRR] 1.51; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.05-2.17; P = 0.03) compared to standard medical treatment. This benefit was not observed in the non-elevated NLR group (26 [41.9%] vs. 25 [38.5%]; aRR 1.12; 95% CI 0.73-1.73). Safety outcomes did not differ in either the elevated or non-elevated NLR groups.

CONCLUSION: Baseline NLR may provide a potential signal for differential treatment response to intravenous tenecteplase in patients with acute ischemic stroke, although these exploratory findings require further validation in independent studies.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: TRACE-III is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05141305.

METHODS: TRACE-III was a phase 3, multicenter, prospective, open-label, randomized, blinded-endpoint trial that enrolled 516 patients from 58 centers in China between January 2022 and November 2023.

title: Translating Stroke Microenvironment Cues Into Materials Design: Intelligent Nanomaterials for Ischemic Stroke Therapy.
abstract: Ischemic stroke (IS), caused by cerebral blood vessel occlusion, leads to ischemia, hypoxia, and irreversible brain tissue damage. Current treatments primarily rely on thrombolytic agents like alteplase, urokinase, and streptokinase for rapid reperfusion. However, these therapies are limited by narrow therapeutic windows, rapid clearance, poor blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, off-target effects, and the complex ischemic microenvironment. These have led to increased interest in nanomaterial-based platforms to improve the precision and efficacy of IS treatment. The IS microenvironment, characterized by oxidative stress, inflammation, ionic imbalance, acidosis, and BBB disruption, provides valuable cues for designing responsive nanomaterials. Nanomaterials engineered to respond to reactive oxygen species, pH, enzymes, light, ultrasound, or magnetic fields can enable targeted drug delivery, controlled release, and multi-modal interventions, enhancing therapeutic precision. This review discusses the IS microenvironment, limitations of traditional therapies, recent advances in intelligent nanomaterials for IS treatment, and the major barriers that currently limit clinical translation.

title: Tenecteplase, alteplase, and endovascular thrombectomy in extended-window acute ischemic stroke with intracranial large-vessel occlusion: a Bayesian network meta-analysis.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: The comparative effects of intravenous thrombolytic agents, endovascular thrombectomy (EVT), and bridging therapy in imaging-selected patients with acute ischemic stroke treated beyond 4.5 hours remain uncertain. We compared these strategies while distinguishing confirmed large-vessel occlusion (LVO) evidence from broader mixed populations.

METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for randomized trials evaluating reperfusion treatments administered 4.5 to 24 hours after stroke onset or last known well. The primary network included trials requiring confirmed intracranial LVO or basilar artery occlusion (BAO). An anterior-circulation LVO network and an all-available network were examined as sensitivity and exploratory analyses. Bayesian random-effects consistency models estimated odds ratios (ORs) with 95% credible intervals (CrIs). The primary outcome was functional independence, defined as a modified Rankin Scale score of 0 to 2 at 90 days.

RESULTS: Fifteen randomized trials were included, of which 8 contributed to the primary confirmed LVO/BAO network. Compared with placebo or best medical care, EVT significantly improved functional independence (OR, 2.93 [95% CrI, 1.40-6.53]) and excellent functional outcome, defined as mRS 0 to 1 (OR, 2.22 [95% CrI, 1.30-4.11]), reduced 90-day mortality (OR, 0.71 [95% CrI, 0.50-0.98]), and increased trial-defined recanalization or reperfusion at approximately 24 hours (OR, 5.27 [95% CrI, 1.83-16.04]); sICH was also increased (OR, 2.65 [95% CrI, 1.28-5.81]). Compared with EVT, tenecteplase plus EVT showed numerically favorable but statistically inconclusive estimates for functional independence (OR, 1.10 [95% CrI, 0.34-3.52]) and excellent outcome (OR, 1.16 [95% CrI, 0.52-2.64]). Direct pairwise analyses of 2 trials were similarly inconclusive. Tenecteplase alone did not show clear differences from placebo or best medical care. Findings were directionally consistent in the anterior-circulation sensitivity and all-available exploratory networks.

CONCLUSIONS: Among imaging-selected patients with confirmed intracranial LVO or BAO treated 4.5 to 24 hours after onset or last known well, EVT had the most consistent evidence of benefit versus placebo or best medical care. Tenecteplase plus EVT showed favorable but imprecise estimates, and neither network nor direct pairwise analyses established superiority over EVT alone. The incremental benefit of bridging tenecteplase remains uncertain.

We compared these strategies while distinguishing confirmed large-vessel occlusion (LVO) evidence from broader mixed populations. METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for randomized trials evaluating reperfusion treatments administered 4.5 to 24 hours after stroke onset or last known well.

title: Immunopathological mechanisms linking atherosclerosis and ischemic stroke: From microenvironmental vulnerability to precision therapeutics.
abstract: Atherosclerotic ischemic stroke results from a multistage process in which systemic susceptibility and local arterial biology converge to generate plaque vulnerability, thrombosis, embolization, and cerebral ischemia. This review critically integrates experimental, human tissue, observational, imaging, and randomized clinical evidence across this continuum. We distinguish disturbed flow-induced endothelial dysfunction and intimal retention of apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins as upstream processes from macrophage dysfunction, defective efferocytosis, vascular smooth muscle cell remodeling, pathological neovascularization, and intraplaque hemorrhage that promote structural vulnerability. We then examine how plaque rupture and, with less direct cerebrovascular evidence, superficial erosion interact with platelet activation, coagulation, and neutrophil-associated immunothrombosis to produce artery-to-artery embolization or hemodynamic ischemia. Systemic modifiers, including clonal hematopoiesis, trained immunity, gut-derived metabolites, psychological stress, infection, and environmental exposures, are evaluated according to evidence maturity and stroke-specific relevance. Poststroke neuroimmune-hematopoietic reprogramming is considered an experimentally supported but incompletely validated feedback mechanism in humans. Among imaging-defined plaque features, carotid intraplaque hemorrhage has comparatively mature human prognostic evidence, whereas many molecular signatures remain investigational. Emerging single-cell, spatial, multiomic, molecular-imaging, and thrombus-profiling technologies are considered separately from clinically validated risk tools. Finally, therapeutic strategies are organized by mechanism and strength of clinical evidence, distinguishing established lipid-lowering, antithrombotic, and reperfusion approaches from investigational inflammatory, lipoprotein(a)-directed, and genome-editing strategies. This evidence-based framework identifies where mechanistic insight is mature, where translation remains uncertain, and how precision prevention may be advanced in atherosclerotic stroke. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: Atherosclerotic ischemic stroke is driven by more than arterial narrowing: plaque vulnerability, immune inflammation, thrombosis, and impaired cerebral perfusion interact to determine clinical risk. By separating findings supported by human cerebrovascular evidence from emerging experimental mechanisms, this review clarifies opportunities and limitations for improved risk stratification, biomarker development, and mechanism-guided prevention.

title: Cerebral Oedema After Ischaemic Stroke: Pathogenesis, Natural History, and Potential Medical Treatments From Bench to Bedside.
abstract: The development of cerebral oedema after ischaemic stroke is a common and potentially devastating complication associated with increased mortality and disability. Despite this, there currently exists no definitive medical treatment for cerebral oedema, and the efficacy of commonly used agents is unclear. In recent decades there has been a significant amount of research attempting to describe the pathogenesis of cerebral oedema in ischaemic stroke which has begun to lead to the development of new potential treatments. In this review we will aim to, firstly, provide a comprehensive overview of the pathogenesis and natural history of cerebral oedema in ischaemic stroke, including cellular mechanisms, breakdown of the blood-brain barrier, the role of the immune system, and potential effects of reperfusion. We will then summarise the evidence base for currently used treatments for cerebral oedema in ischaemic stroke such as hyperosmolar agents, as well as emerging treatments which are still under investigation. Where available, this review will highlight outcomes of clinical trials for these proposed treatments.

title: Integrated multi-omics reveals gut microbiota-metabolic mechanisms underlying the neuroprotective effects of Xijiao Dihuang Decoction against cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) remains a major barrier to functional recovery after reperfusion therapy for ischemic stroke. Increasing evidence indicates that gut microbiota dysbiosis and metabolic disturbance are closely involved in post-stroke neuroinflammation and secondary brain injury. Xijiao Dihuang Decoction (XDD), a classical traditional Chinese medicine formula, has shown protective effects in cerebrovascular disorders; however, whether its effects against CIRI are associated with coordinated regulation of the gut microbiota and host metabolism remains unclear.

METHODS: Circulating XDD-derived components were characterized by ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS). Network pharmacology and molecular docking were used to predict potential targets and signaling pathways associated with CIRI. A middle cerebral artery occlusion/reperfusion (MCAO/R) rat model was established, and rats were treated with low-, medium-, or high-dose XDD for 7 days, with edaravone as a positive control. Neurological deficits, cerebral infarct volume, hemorheological parameters, histopathological changes, and serum inflammatory cytokines were assessed. Cecal microbiota composition was analyzed by 16S rDNA sequencing, and cecal metabolic profiles were investigated using untargeted LC-MS metabolomics. Multi-omics integration and Spearman correlation analysis were performed to explore associations between differentially abundant bacterial genera and characteristic metabolites.

RESULTS: A total of 54 XDD-derived circulating components were identified. Network pharmacology analysis indicated that the putative targets of XDD were mainly enriched in pathways related to inflammation, lipid and energy metabolism, and regulated cell death, with AKT1 and NLRP3 were predicted as potential hub targets. In MCAO/R rats, XDD improved neurological deficits, reduced cerebral infarct volume, alleviated hemorheological abnormalities, and attenuated neuronal injury. XDD also reduced serum IL-6 levels and lowered IL-1β levels mainly at medium and high doses. In addition, XDD partially restored gut microbial diversity and remodeled CIRI-associated microbial dysbiosis. Metabolomics analysis revealed marked metabolic disturbances after MCAO/R, and XDD reversed part of these alterations, particularly those related to lipid metabolism. Integrated analysis further linked specific bacterial genera with lipid mediators and fatty acid-related metabolites, indicating coordinated remodeling of the gut microbiota and host metabolism.

CONCLUSION: XDD exerts neuroprotective effects against CIRI through multi-target and multi-pathway actions. Its therapeutic effects may be associated with coordinated regulation of gut microbial homeostasis, metabolic reprogramming, and inflammatory/cell death signaling. These findings provide new evidence supporting the potential application of XDD in ischemic stroke and offer insight into microbiota-related mechanisms underlying its neuroprotective effects.

title: Clinical Characteristics and In-Hospital Course of Symptomatic Intracranial Hemorrhage After Intravenous Alteplase in Older Adults with Acute Ischemic Stroke: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
abstract: Background/Objectives: This study describes symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (sICH) after intravenous alteplase in older adults with acute ischemic stroke. Methods: This retrospective single-center cohort included 95 unique patients aged ≥65 years treated in Galati, Romania, in 2020-2024. The binary hemorrhage variable was verified against clinical and computed tomography (CT) records. Study-defined sICH required new or increased CT hemorrhage with attributed deterioration, comprising a ≥4-point National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) increase or other clinically relevant worsening. Comparisons and Firth models were exploratory, with admission NIHSS adjustment. Results: All 14 recorded hemorrhages met this definition (14.7%; 95% CI 9.0-23.2%): 10 met the NIHSS threshold and four had relevant worsening below it. Ten were detected before 24 h and four at the 24-48 h range; morphology included hemorrhagic infarction and parenchymal hematoma. All adjusted intervals included the null. Median hospitalization was five days longer with sICH. The mortality difference was 2.6 percentage points (conservative exact 95% CI range from -31.6 to 45.9). Conclusions: Adjusted association estimates are inconclusive and do not justify altering guideline-based eligibility. Prospective multicenter studies require standardized definitions, stroke-severity measures, reperfusion data, and functional outcomes.

title: High-frequency rTMS attenuates cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury and modulates mTOR-related signaling and brain-gut-immune phenotypes in MCAO/R rats.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: High-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) may promote neurological recovery after ischemic stroke, but its protective effects after MCAO/R and associations with neurotrophic factors, mTOR-related autophagy markers, systemic inflammation, and gut microbiota phenotypes remain unclear.

METHODS: Cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury was induced by right MCAO/R. Rats were assigned to Sham, MCAO/R, and MCAO/R + high-frequency rTMS groups. rTMS was initiated on postoperative day 3. Neurological and motor functions were assessed behaviorally. Western blotting, immunofluorescence, ELISA, and 16S rRNA sequencing were used to examine related proteins, inflammatory cytokines, and gut microbiota, followed by multivariate and correlation analyses.

RESULTS: High-frequency rTMS improved neurological and motor functions, reduced infarction and histopathological injury, decreased TUNEL positivity, and increased the number of Nissl-positive neurons. It upregulated FGF-2, BDNF, and the p-mTOR (Ser2448)/mTOR ratio, attenuated abnormal changes in Beclin-1, LC3-II/LC3-I, and p62, and reduced serum TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6 levels. 16S rRNA sequencing showed altered gut microbiota β-diversity and genus-level composition, with several genera associated with motor or inflammatory indices.

CONCLUSION: High-frequency rTMS alleviated cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury and promoted neurological recovery after MCAO/R, accompanied by enhanced neurotrophic support, improvement in mTOR-related autophagy marker abnormalities, and lower serum pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. Gut microbiota alterations were also observed following rTMS treatment, although their functional significance remains exploratory.

METHODS: Cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury was induced by right MCAO/R. Rats were assigned to Sham, MCAO/R, and MCAO/R + high-frequency rTMS groups.

title: FLAIR vascular hyperintensities in acute ischemic stroke: from collateral-related imaging findings to a candidate dynamic hemodynamic imaging phenotype.
abstract: With advances in reperfusion therapies for acute large vessel occlusion (LVO), stroke imaging evaluation has progressively shifted from time-based treatment selection toward comprehensive assessment of tissue status and hemodynamic adaptation. However, current imaging approaches primarily characterize vascular patency, perfusion status, and tissue injury, while remaining limited in their ability to directly capture the dynamic regulatory processes of cerebral circulation after arterial occlusion. In patients with LVO, ischemic tissue outcome is determined not only by the occlusion site and time to reperfusion but also by collateral circulation capacity, cerebral hemodynamic status, and tissue tolerance to ischemia. Therefore, imaging biomarkers capable of reflecting cerebral circulatory adaptation under ischemic conditions are of substantial research interest. FLAIR vascular hyperintensities (FVHs) are MRI findings characterized by linear or serpentine hyperintense signals along the cortical surface, within cortical sulci, or along the Sylvian fissure on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequences. They are generally associated with reduced distal blood flow velocity, prolonged blood transit time, and hemodynamic alterations mediated by leptomeningeal collateral pathways. In recent years, numerous studies have investigated the role of FVHs in the diagnosis of acute ischemic stroke, evaluation of reperfusion therapy, and prediction of clinical outcomes. However, the clinical significance of FVHs remains incompletely understood. Some studies have suggested that FVHs are associated with favorable collateral status and smaller infarct volumes, whereas others have demonstrated that FVHs may also occur in patients with more pronounced hemodynamic impairment. These discrepancies suggest that FVHs may not simply represent favorable collateral circulation or ischemic severity, but may instead reflect the dynamic hemodynamic response of the cerebral circulation to reduced perfusion following arterial occlusion. From the perspective of precision stroke imaging, this review systematically summarizes the mechanisms underlying FVH formation, their biological significance, and clinical implications. Particular emphasis is placed on the relationships between FVHs and collateral circulation, FVHs-DWI mismatch, ischemic tissue status, and potential benefit from reperfusion therapy. Furthermore, current challenges related to FVH standardization and clinical translation are discussed, with particular emphasis on their potential role as a candidate dynamic hemodynamic imaging phenotype reflecting physiological hemodynamic adaptation.

title: Tongxinluo is associated with neurovascular changes following rt-PA-treated ischemic stroke: associations with inflammation, vascular remodeling, and neural plasticity.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rt-PA) is the standard treatment for acute ischemic stroke but is often limited by microvascular obstruction and reperfusion injury. Tongxinluo (TXL) has demonstrated neuroprotective potential, yet its association with neurovascular responses during rt-PA-associated reperfusion remains incompletely characterized.

METHODS: Because reperfusion was achieved by filament withdrawal before rt-PA administration, this model evaluates TXL-associated effects during mechanically induced reperfusion with rt-PA exposure rather than enhancement of rt-PA-mediated thrombolysis. Animals were randomized into Sham, MCAO, MCAO + rt-PA, and MCAO + rt-PA + TXL (low/high dose) groups. Neurological outcomes were assessed longitudinally. Cerebral perfusion was monitored using laser speckle contrast imaging (LSCI). Mechanistic analyses included assessments of blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, oxidative stress, microglial activation, angiogenesis, mitochondrial function, apoptosis, and synaptic plasticity markers (BDNF, GAP-43, and Synapsin I) using histological, biochemical, and molecular techniques.

RESULTS: Adjunctive TXL treatment was associated with improved neurological outcomes and reduced infarct volume compared with rt-PA alone, with dose-dependent trends observed. TXL was associated with improved cortical microvascular perfusion and reduced severity of the no-reflow phenomenon. Mechanistically, TXL suppressed microglia-mediated neuroinflammation (downregulating TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6) and preserved BBB integrity. This anti-inflammatory environment facilitated angiogenic maturation, evidenced by increased microvessel density and lumen formation. Furthermore, TXL stabilized mitochondrial function, inhibited neuronal apoptosis, and upregulated BDNF, GAP-43, and Synapsin I, leading to significant restoration of dendritic spine density.

CONCLUSION: TXL may provide adjunctive neuroprotective effects in the context of rt-PA treatment by modulating inflammatory, vascular-associated, and neuronal recovery responses. These findings support further investigation of TXL as a complementary therapy following reperfusion. By concurrently suppressing neuroinflammation and promoting vascular and synaptic reconstruction, TXL translates multi-target modulation into robust functional recovery, supporting its potential as a strategic combination therapy for acute ischemic stroke.
